newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein calls for place at N.Irish talks.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein calls for place at N.Irish talks.

text.p: The chief strategist of the IRA's political arm urged Britain on Monday to bring his Sinn Fein party into Northern Ireland peace talks to stem fears of a new cycle of violence by the province's rival guerrilla groups.

"I believe that 1997 is going to be a defining year in the history of the politics of this island. There are two roads to travel, one is the road to the negotiating table and the other is the road to further conflict," Martin McGuinness told BBC radio.
"We have already seen in the course of recent weeks a slide back into conflict. That needs to be arrested. The road that Sinn Fein wants to travel is the road to the negotating table."
Britain says a 17-month truce which the Irish Republican Army (IRA) -- fighting to oust Britain from Northern Ireland -- abandoned last February was a sham.
It is adamant that Sinn Fein will not be given a seat at multiparty peace talks until the guerrillas declare a lasting and "credible" ceasefire.

Sinn Fein maintains that Britain's ruling Conservatives, who have lost their overall parliamentary majority, are barring it from the talks to buy vital support from Protestant legislators who speak for the province's pro-British majority.
The security climate has deteriorated in the past two weeks with signs that the IRA's bitter enemy, so-called Loyalist guerrillas, have broken a two-year-old ceasefire.
Local media reports quoting unidentified "informed sources" say that Loyalist militants, out to avenge recent IRA attacks, were responsible for two attempts to kill senior republicans.
Loyalist commanders have refused to comment and parties linked to them say that as far as they are aware the truce is still intact.
One republican supporter was wounded when his booby-trapped vehicle exploded but the second intended victim spotted a bomb under his car and British army technical officers defused it.
Renewed Loyalist violence would be critically dangerous for the province's desperate search for a peaceful way forward after years of strife over British rule.

McGuinness, who has been Sinn Fein's chief negotiator in previous exploratory talks with the British, again denied a British press reports that he and his party president Gerry Adams had recently become members of the IRA's army council.
He said a three-year peace process that has floundered amid IRA violence and bitter political rivalries between pro-British Protestant and pro-Irish Catholic parties should be rebuilt.
The London Times said on Monday the IRA had a new "hawkish" chief-of-staff whose appointement has triggered intensive British security precautions.
"The police and (internal security) MI5...are fully prepared for a terrorist campaign in the new year," the Times said.
